o: Heavenly Father, I begin this day by thanking You for Your faithfulness. Your mercy is renewed every morning and Your Word endures forever. Thank You for the freedom to pray, for having Your Bible within reach and for the hope You give me when circumstances are not easy.

Lord, I want to learn to love Your Word more than anything else. You know that sometimes I become discouraged when trials drag on and I see no way out. But Your law is better to me than thousands of pieces of gold and silver. Give me a heart that perseveres, that does not grow cold in the face of difficulty and that keeps trusting in You to the end.

Bless today those who suffer because of their faith and those deprived of freedom, for whatever reason. Console them by Your presence and strengthen their hope. Take care of my family, guide my decisions and help me be a faithful witness of Your love in every place. May my words and actions give a good testimony of You. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 12, 1660, the English preacher John Bunyan was arrested for preaching without official authorization. Bunyan was born in 1628 near Bedford and worked as a tinker, that is, he mended pots and metal utensils. After a profound experience of faith, he became a preacher greatly loved by the ordinary people of his region.

But the times had changed in England. With the return of the monarchy, religious meetings were required to be held within the official Church, and preaching outside of it was considered an offense. Bunyan was preaching at a farmhouse called Lower Samsell, near Harlington, when he was warned that there was a warrant against him. He was able to flee, but decided to stay and be brought before the magistrate.

In January 1661, he was tried in Bedford. He was offered freedom if he promised to stop preaching, but he refused, convinced that he could not be silent about what God had entrusted to him. He ended up spending about twelve years in prison, until 1672. It was a hard time for his family, who depended on him for their living.

Yet those years bore fruit. In prison he wrote “Grace Abounding,” a moving account of his spiritual life published in 1666, and began to write “The Pilgrim's Progress,” which was published in 1678 and became one of the most widely read books of Christian literature. His story reminds us that no prison can chain the Word of God or extinguish the faith of one who trusts in him.
m.c: May the Lord sustain you today with his strong hand and remind you that his Word is not chained. Walk with courage, confident that every trial has its purpose in his hands. May his faithfulness accompany you at every step of the day.
m: The story of John Bunyan leaves us with an important question: what do we do when circumstances are not what we expected? He could have chosen bitterness, silence or abandoning his faith. Instead he chose to remain faithful, and his prison became a place where the Word of God took deeper root in his heart.

Psalm 119 says: “It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes. The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces.” The psalmist does not say that suffering is pleasant, but that God can use it to teach us something we would not otherwise learn. When everything else shifts, we discover what truly sustains us.

Jesus himself warned that the love of many would grow cold in times of difficulty, but he promised: “The one who endures to the end will be saved.” Persevering does not mean feeling no weariness; it means continuing forward with God's help, step by step. Today you may not be facing prison, but perhaps you are facing an illness, a conflict or a long wait. In that place too, you can learn to trust.

Apply it in a simple way. Choose a verse of the Bible and repeat it during the day, every time you feel discouragement. If you can, write it on a piece of paper and carry it with you. Speak with someone going through a trial and offer them your company. And when you feel your strength running out, remember Bunyan: in his cell, God gave him words that have consoled millions of people. In your situation too, God can do something beautiful.

t.s: The Father of the Tormented Boy
o: Lord Jesus, I end this day with gratitude in my heart. Thank You for accompanying me at every moment, for the strength You gave me and for the blessings I sometimes did not notice, but which were with me. You are good and forgiving, and abounding in mercy to all who call upon You.

There are things I did not understand today and situations I could not settle. My faith is sometimes weak and filled with doubts. But I come to You with sincerity, like that father who said to You: I believe; help my unbelief. Strengthen my trust, Lord. Do not allow fear to have the last word, and teach me to rest on Your power, which can do all things.

I now give You my family and my loved ones. Care for the sick, comfort the grieving and give hope to parents who pray for their children. Give me quiet sleep and a mind at peace. At dawn, may my faith be stronger than yesterday and may my heart rejoice in You. Thank You for always listening to me. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: When Jesus came down from the mountain with Peter, James and John, he found a great crowd around his disciples and scribes arguing with them. A man came out of the crowd and explained what was happening: he had brought his son, who suffered from an affliction that had tormented him since childhood, and the disciples had not been able to help.

The father was weary and wounded by years of anguish. When Jesus asked him how long this had been happening, he explained with pain what he had been through, and said to him: “If you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” Then Jesus answered him with words full of power: “If you can! All things are possible for one who believes.”

This man did not respond with grand speeches. With tears, he cried out one of the most sincere prayers in the Bible: “I believe; help my unbelief!” He did not pretend to have perfect faith. He acknowledged that he had faith, but that he also had doubts, and he asked Jesus to help him with both. Jesus did not rebuke him for it.

Then Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, and the boy became like a corpse, so that many said he was dead. But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he stood. This story consoles us because it shows us that we do not need perfect faith to come to Christ. It is enough to come to him sincerely. He receives our little faith and helps us grow.
t.c: As you end this day, give thanks for what God has done for you and hand over what still worries you. His hand lifts you up and his mercy covers you without your having to strive. Sleep in peace and wake full of renewed hope.
m: Psalm 86 affirms: “For you, Lord, are good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you.” These words are a treasure for the night, when we take stock of what has been lived. Perhaps we remember mistakes, doubts or fears that accompanied us. Yet the God to whom we pray forgives and is attentive to the voice of our pleas.

The story of the boy's father offers us a prayer we can pray any night: “I believe; help my unbelief.” It is an honest prayer, and God loves honesty. Many people think faith consists in not having the slightest doubt, but the Bible shows us that authentic faith sometimes lives alongside questions, and that God helps us move forward while we wait.

Tonight, instead of reproaching yourself for the times you doubted, do something different. Think of a concrete situation in which you struggle to trust: someone's health, work, a family matter. Tell God exactly what you feel. Then calmly repeat the father's prayer. The circumstances may not change this very night, but your heart will begin to rest.

Remember also that Jesus took the boy by the hand and lifted him up. He continues to take by the hand those who feel fallen. Before sleeping, stretch out your hand in prayer and accept his help. Give thanks for what you saw rightly of God today, however small, and believe that tomorrow his power will continue to work. With this certainty, you can close your eyes in peace.
